units.title: Smooth positive approximation of a measurable time coefficient
units.statement: For every measurable coefficient with the stated almost-everywhere range on \([a,b]\), there is a globally smooth real function \(g\) that is strictly positive and at most \(C+\varepsilon\) at every point of that interval, and whose integrated absolute error is less than \(\varepsilon\).
units.formula: \exists g\in C^\infty(\mathbb R),\quad 0<g(t)\le C+\varepsilon\ (a\le t\le b),\qquad \int_a^b |g(t)-f(t)|\,dt<\varepsilon.
assumptions: The endpoints \(a,b\) are real with \(a\le b\). All integrals are Lebesgue integrals restricted to the closed interval \([a,b]\). The case \(a=b\) is included.
The constants satisfy \(C\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). The function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is Borel measurable.
The range condition \(0\le f(t)\le C\) holds almost everywhere on \([a,b]\). No condition is placed on its values outside that interval or on its exceptional null set.
units.boundary: The approximation is for one prescribed finite interval and tolerance. Smoothness holds on all of \(\mathbb R\); positivity and the displayed upper bound are guaranteed on \([a,b]\). This result controls coefficient integrals. Convergence of solutions and passage of density estimates to limits require further arguments.

proof.title: Approximate by a bounded continuous function
proof.text: The finite interval and the bound on \(f\) give integrability. Apply continuous approximation with half the error budget.

proof.title: Clip the continuous approximation to the allowed range
proof.text: Set \(u(t)=\max(0,\min(C,q(t)))\). This is continuous and takes values in \([0,C]\) everywhere. Projection onto this interval cannot increase the distance to an almost-everywhere value of \(f\).

proof.title: Smooth on a compact neighborhood
proof.text: Write \(L=b-a\) and choose \(\delta=\varepsilon/[4(L+1)]\). Uniform continuity on the compact closed one-neighborhood of the interval lets the smooth approximation theorem produce a globally smooth \(v\) with the required error on the interval.

proof.title: Shift to obtain strict positivity
proof.text: Set \(g=v+\delta\). Since \(0\le u\le C\), the shift gives strict positivity. The estimate \(2\delta\le\varepsilon\) also gives the claimed upper bound. Boundedness on the finite interval yields all integral expressions used below.

proof.title: Add the two error budgets
proof.text: The smoothing and shift cost at most \(2\delta L<\varepsilon/2\) in integral. The triangle inequality combines this with the clipped approximation.

units.title: One approximation for a coefficient and its noise amplitude
units.statement: Under the same assumptions there is one globally smooth function \(g\), positive and at most \(C+\varepsilon\) on \([a,b]\), for which both the integrated coefficient error and the integrated squared error of the noise amplitude \(\sqrt{2f}\) are less than \(\varepsilon\).
assumptions: The endpoints \(a,b\) are real with \(a\le b\). All integrals are Lebesgue integrals restricted to the closed interval \([a,b]\). The case \(a=b\) is included.
The constants satisfy \(C\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). The function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is Borel measurable.
The range condition \(0\le f(t)\le C\) holds almost everywhere on \([a,b]\). No condition is placed on its values outside that interval or on its exceptional null set.
units.boundary: The approximation is for one prescribed finite interval and tolerance. Smoothness holds on all of \(\mathbb R\); positivity and the displayed upper bound are guaranteed on \([a,b]\). This result controls coefficient integrals. Convergence of solutions and passage of density estimates to limits require further arguments.

proof.title: Use the coefficient theorem at half tolerance
proof.text: Choose the same \(g\) from the preceding result with tolerance \(\varepsilon/2\). Its pointwise upper bound is even \(C+\varepsilon/2\), and both coefficient functions are integrable.

proof.title: Compare square roots without a positive lower bound
proof.text: For nonnegative \(x,y\), split into \(x\le y\) and \(y\le x\), expand the square, and use monotonicity of square root. This proves the estimate even when either input is zero.

proof.title: Integrate the pointwise comparison
proof.text: Apply that inequality to \(x=2g(t)\), \(y=2f(t)\) almost everywhere. The squared noise error is measurable and dominated by an integrable coefficient error, so it is integrable. Integration gives the strict error bound for the same \(g\).
